courseReview.cachedDescription: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
courseReview.assessment: Brain and behaviour overview; no evidenced sustained parent, school, pedagogy or educational-intervention study.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseReview.assessment: Sociology, race, class and gender inform child social environments, but no child-specific pedagogical study.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Introduces cells, molecular biology, cellular physiology and communication. It connects genetic information and variation with living systems and offers initial perspectives on life sciences, biomedicine and public health. A research presentation develops engagement with scientific literature.
courseReview.assessment: Cell and molecular gateway; foundational life science, not an education or child-development course.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.
courseReview.assessment: Epidemiological research in public health, not parenting or educational science.

courseReview.cachedDescription: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseReview.assessment: The UCR Year-1 PPD requirement; academic and personal formation, not disciplinary pedagogical content.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
courseReview.assessment: Evolutionary and animal brain neurobiology; absence of child/education framing matters for the claimed biological-foundations correspondence.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
courseReview.assessment: History of gender and inequality; no documented central child-upbringing/educational-practice study.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
courseReview.assessment: Actual work with primary-school pupils on persuasive speaking, but it teaches rhetoric rather than curriculum design or pedagogy theory.

courseReview.cachedDescription: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courseReview.assessment: Statistical models and empirical methods; useful for pedagogical research but not specifically psychometrics or learning research.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
courseReview.assessment: Human organ systems and physiology; not established as child-development or learning biology.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
courseReview.assessment: Ethical persuasion and climate messaging with climate-science partners. NOT a course in school communication or educational design.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courseReview.assessment: Social theory, imperialism, colonial responses and modernity; actual description does not establish substantial socialisation and educational inequality content.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
courseReview.assessment: Neural mechanisms of sensory perception and action, not educational intervention.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
courseReview.assessment: Substantive human development across life stages, including early life and social/cognitive/emotional development; narrower than Erasmus's pedagogy-plus-personality course.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.
courseReview.assessment: General psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy, not specialist parenting support, family intervention or pedagogical professional practice.

courseReview.cachedDescription: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
courseReview.assessment: Systematic review and meta-analysis, not a pedagogical bachelor project or primary intervention design.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
courseReview.assessment: Higher-order cognitive/neural functioning and experimental tasks, not pedagogy as an organising domain.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
courseReview.assessment: Evidence-based youth resilience with schools/educators; a genuine educational-setting project but focused on extremism and wellbeing, not broad parent support.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courseReview.assessment: Civil-society theory and NGO projects; possible social-context application but no documented parenting or school emphasis.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
courseReview.assessment: Biopsychosocial health psychology, medically framed rather than parenting or education.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
courseReview.assessment: General social psychology informs child social environments but does not itself study pedagogical practice.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
courseReview.assessment: Mental disorders, assessment and biopsychosocial treatment; relevant to developmental difficulties but no documented orthopedagogical child/family focus.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
courseReview.assessment: Language acquisition, reading/dyslexia and neuropsychological language study genuinely touch learning but not curriculum design or education science.

courseReview.cachedDescription: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseReview.assessment: General qualitative social research; supports methods but not subject-specific qualitative learning-study design.

repairExploration.gap: Official Erasmus outcomes require continuing parenting/upbringing theory, education-science conceptual models, school/pedagogical practice, prevention/diagnosis in pedagogical context and discipline-specific research. Selected UCR options are dominated by cognitive neuroscience, clinical/general psychology and sociology; isolated school/youth examples do not establish that programme-level inquiry.
repairExploration.provisionalJudgment: Existing positive UCR comparison is academically unsupported on inspected source/cache evidence. Before authorising a no-defensible-match exception, inspect complete enriched course workbook and test bounded viable reconstruction rather than infer absence from cache.

schedulingObservations: Exactly four 7.5-EC courses appear in every semester and 24 distinct courses are selected; this is static canonical structure, not a new feasibility replay.
Introduction to Social Psychology (HCBPSYC111) is scheduled in semester six, after multiple higher-level psychology courses; substantive advisory progression deserves review.
Qualitative Research Methodology (GOSSOCI212) is in semester six, after the Advanced Research Seminar (HCBPSYC313) in semester four; sequencing deserves review.
UCR Year-1 PPD ACCPPDE101 appears in semester two; hard prerequisite and term availability require actual enriched workbook check.
